parts.latex:
The lamp shown in the diagram below can move along the vertical line $OB$ using a pulley system. The point $A$ lies on the horizontal line $OA$ at a distance of $d$ from $O$. The intensity $I$ of light from the lamp at point $A$ is inversely proportional to the square of its distance $r$ from the lamp. The intensity $I$ is also directly proportional to $\sin\phi$, where $\phi$ is the angle of elevation from $A$ to the lamp. Hence, the formula for $I$ can be expressed as:
$$I=\dfrac{C\sin\phi}{r^2}, \quad \text{where } C \text{ is a positive constant.}$$
Determine the height $h$ of the lamp above the line $OA$ that maximizes the intensity of light at the point $A$. Express your answer in terms of $d$.

\exfigure{408_q31_1}

solutions.latex:
The lamp is $h$ above $O$ and $A$ is $d$ from $O$, so $O$, $A$ and the lamp form a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $r$. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$r^2 = h^2 + d^2$$
$\phi$ is the angle at $A$, and the side opposite it is $h$:
$$\sin\phi = \dfrac{h}{r} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+d^2}}$$
Substitute both into $I = \dfrac{C\sin\phi}{r^2}$ to write $I$ in terms of $h$ only:
$$\begin{aligned} I &= C\left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+d^2}}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{h^2+d^2}\right) \\ &= Ch(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
Differentiate using the product rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dI}{dh} &= C(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{3}{2}} + Ch\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right)(2h)(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}} \\ &= C(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}}\left[(h^2+d^2) - 3h^2\right] \\ &= C(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}}(d^2 - 2h^2) \end{aligned}$$
Since $C>0$ and $(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}}>0$, $\dfrac{dI}{dh}=0$ when
$$\begin{aligned} d^2 - 2h^2 &= 0 \\ h^2 &= \dfrac{d^2}{2} \\ h &= \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}d \quad (h>0) \end{aligned}$$
The sign of $\dfrac{dI}{dh}$ is the sign of $d^2-2h^2$. Test either side:
$$\begin{aligned} h &= \dfrac{d}{2}: & d^2-2\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^2 &= \dfrac{d^2}{2} > 0 \\ h &= d: & d^2-2d^2 &= -d^2 < 0 \end{aligned}$$
$I$ increases then decreases, so the stationary point is a maximum.

$\therefore$ The intensity at $A$ is greatest when $h = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}d$.
criteria: Makes a suitable substitution, $\sin\phi=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+d^2}}$, or equivalent merit

$$\therefore\ BE = \dfrac{\sqrt{400 - x^2}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{400 - x^2}$$

Set $\dfrac{dA}{dx} = 0$: since $0 < x < 20$, $x + 20 \neq 0$, so $x = 10$.

99.stem: A right circular cone has height, $H$, and a base of radius $R$. A square prism is inscribed in the cone so that the base of the prism is on the cone's base. The prism has height, $h$, and a square base of side length $x$. \exfigure{1365_q30_1}

figures.cap: cone with inscribed square prism, and cross-section showing H and R

parts.latex: By using similar triangles, show that $x=2R\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right)$.
Determine the height of the prism, in terms of $H$, that will maximise the volume of the prism.

solutions.latex:
In the cross-section, the triangle above the prism (height $H-h$, base $\dfrac{x}{2}$) is similar to the whole right-angled triangle (height $H$, base $R$): common angle at the apex, both right-angled (equiangular).
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{H-h}{H} &= \dfrac{\frac{x}{2}}{R} \\ x &= 2R\left(\dfrac{H-h}{H}\right) \\ &= 2R\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right) \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Be careful that the correct ratio is used.
meta.top_criterion_original: Correct ratio. Do NOT need any geometric reasoning
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the question named the radius $r$ but part (a) and this working use $R$; the question now says $R$.
meta.explained: Similar-triangle reasoning explained in words (owner request, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} V &= x^2h \\ &= \left(2R\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right)\right)^2h \\ &= 4R^2h\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right)^2 \\ &= 4R^2h\left(1-\dfrac{2h}{H}+\dfrac{h^2}{H^2}\right) \\ &= 4R^2h-\dfrac{8R^2h^2}{H}+\dfrac{4R^2h^3}{H^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dV}{dh}=4R^2-\dfrac{16R^2h}{H}+\dfrac{12R^2h^2}{H^2}$$
For stationary points, $\dfrac{dV}{dh}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4R^2\left(1-\dfrac{4h}{H}+\dfrac{3h^2}{H^2}\right) &= 0 \\ 4R^2\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right)\left(1-\dfrac{3h}{H}\right) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h=H \text{ or } h=\dfrac{H}{3}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dh^2}=-\dfrac{16R^2}{H}+\dfrac{24R^2h}{H^2}$$
At $h=H$:
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dh^2}=\dfrac{8R^2}{H}>0$$
$\therefore$ concave up.

At $h=\dfrac{H}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2V}{dh^2} &= -\dfrac{16R^2}{H}+\dfrac{24R^2(\frac{H}{3})}{H^2} \\ &= -\dfrac{16R^2}{H}+\dfrac{8R^2}{H} \\ &= -\dfrac{8R^2}{H}<0 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ concave down.

$\therefore\ h=\dfrac{H}{3}$ is a maximum.
criteria: Finds $V$ in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit

522.stem: A piece of wire is 100 cm long. Some of the wire is to be used to make a circle of radius $r$ cm. The remainder of the wire is used to make an equilateral triangle of side length $x$ cm.

parts.latex:
Show that the combined area of the circle and equilateral triangle is given by

$$A(x)=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\sqrt{3}x^2+\dfrac{(100-3x)^2}{\pi}\right).$$
By considering the quadratic function in part (a), show that the maximum value of $A(x)$ occurs when all the wire is used for the circle.

solutions.latex:
The circumference of the circle and the perimeter of the triangle add to 100 cm:
$$2\pi r+3x=100$$
$$r=\dfrac{100-3x}{2\pi}$$
Area of circle $\pi r^2$; area of the equilateral triangle $\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin 60^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} A(x) &= \text{Area of circle}+\text{area of equilateral triangle} \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin 60^\circ \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}x^2 \\ &= \pi\left(\dfrac{100-3x}{2\pi}\right)^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}x^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\sqrt{3}\,x^2+\dfrac{(100-3x)^2}{\pi}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds an expression for $r$ in terms of $x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$A(x)$ is a quadratic with positive coefficient of $x^2$, so $A$ has a minimum stationary point.

The maximum will therefore occur at an endpoint of the domain.

When $x=0$ (all wire used for the circle):
$$r=\dfrac{50}{\pi}$$
$$\text{Area}=\pi r^2=\dfrac{50^2}{\pi}\approx 796$$
When $r=0$ (all wire used for the triangle):
$$x=33\dfrac{1}{3}$$
$$\text{Area}=\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin 60^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\times 33.333^2\approx 481$$
\exfigure{1630_q26_s1}

$\therefore$ The maximum value of $A(x)$ occurs when all wire is used for the circle.

parts.latex: Show that the first derivative of $g(x)=\dfrac{x}{\ln x}$ is $g'(x)=\dfrac{\ln x-1}{(\ln x)^2}$.
What is the global maximum of $g(x)$ on the interval $[2,5]$?

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x)&=\dfrac{1\cdot\ln x-x\cdot\frac{1}{x}}{(\ln x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{\ln x-1}{(\ln x)^2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly applies the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Numerical derivative at x=3 matches formula.

solutions.latex:
Stationary points: $g'(x)=0$ when $\ln x-1=0$, so $x=e$, which lies in $[2,5]$.

The denominator $(\ln x)^2>0$, so the sign of $g'(x)$ is decided by $\ln x-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x)&<0 &&\text{for } 2\le x<e &&\text{decreasing}\\ g'(x)&>0 &&\text{for } e<x\le5 &&\text{increasing}\end{aligned}$$
So $x=e$ is a local minimum, and the global maximum is at an endpoint:
$$\begin{aligned} g(2)&=\dfrac{2}{\ln2}\approx2.885\\ g(5)&=\dfrac{5}{\ln5}\approx3.107\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the global maximum is } \dfrac{5}{\ln5}\approx3.11 \text{ (at } x=5)$$
criteria: Shows $x=e$ is a minimum and evaluates $g$ at an endpoint, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary point at $x=e$, or equivalent merit

The rectangle has sides $QR=2x$ and $RS=y$:

From part (a), $(x+y)^2=36-4x^2$ and $x+y>0$, so $x+y=\sqrt{36-4x^2}$.

parts.latex: Find two expressions in terms of $\theta$, one expression for the time taken for the bus to travel from $S$ to $P$ and the other expression for the time taken by Lucas to cycle from $F$ to $P$.

By considering the difference in the time taken for the bus and Lucas to travel to $P$, find the latest time that Lucas can leave home in order to catch the bus? Give your answer to the nearest minute.

solutions.latex:
In right-angled $\triangle FGP$, $FG=300$ and $\angle GFP=\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\theta&=\dfrac{GP}{FG}\\&=\dfrac{GP}{300}\\GP&=300\tan\theta\end{aligned}$$
The bus travels $SP=4000+GP$ at 20 m/s, and time $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_B&=\dfrac{4000+300\tan\theta}{20}\\&=200+15\tan\theta\end{aligned}$$
Lucas cycles $FP$ at 8 m/s:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\theta&=\dfrac{FG}{FP}\\&=\dfrac{300}{FP}\\FP&=\dfrac{300}{\cos\theta}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}T_L&=\dfrac{300}{\cos\theta}\div 8\\&=\dfrac{75}{2\cos\theta}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the time taken for either the bus or Lucas to make their journey OR correctly writes an expression for $GP$ and $FP$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Lucas can leave home $T=T_B-T_L$ seconds after 8 am and still reach $P$ in time, so the latest departure is when this difference is a maximum.
$$T=200+15\tan\theta-\dfrac{75}{2\cos\theta}$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dT}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=200+15\tan\theta-\dfrac{75}{2}(\cos\theta)^{-1}\\T'&=15\sec^2\theta+\dfrac{75}{2}(\cos\theta)^{-2}\times(-\sin\theta)\\&=\dfrac{15}{\cos^2\theta}-\dfrac{75\sin\theta}{2\cos^2\theta}\\0&=\dfrac{15}{\cos^2\theta}-\dfrac{75\sin\theta}{2\cos^2\theta}\\0&=15-\dfrac{75}{2}\sin\theta\\\dfrac{75}{2}\sin\theta&=15\\\sin\theta&=\dfrac{30}{75}\\\theta&=0.4115168461\end{aligned}$$
Check the sign of $T'$ either side of $\theta=0.411\ldots$:

\exfigure{1356_q33_s1}

$T'$ changes from positive to negative, so $T$ is a maximum when $\theta=0.411\ldots$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=200+15\tan\theta-\dfrac{75}{2\cos\theta}\\&=165.6306823\text{ seconds}\\&=2\text{ minutes and }45\text{ seconds}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Lucas must leave at 8:02 am at the very latest to catch the bus.

$ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezium, with three equal sides, $AD=DC=CB=12$ cm, as shown in the diagam below. The length of $BQ=x$.

figures.cap: isosceles trapezium ABCD with DC=12 cm, height h from C to Q on AB, BQ=x; NOT TO SCALE

parts.latex: Show that the area of $ABCD$ is given by $A=(12+x)\sqrt{144-x^2}\text{ cm}^2$.
Hence find the value of $x$ when the area of the trapezium is a maximum.

solutions.latex:
Pythagoras' theorem in right-angled $\triangle BQC$ (hypotenuse $CB=12$, base $BQ=x$):
$$h=\sqrt{144-x^2}$$
The trapezium is isosceles, so $AB$ is $DC=12$ plus $x$ at each end:
$$AB=12+2x$$
Area of a trapezium, $A=\dfrac{1}{2}h(a+b)$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\sqrt{144-x^2}\times(12+12+2x)\\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{144-x^2}}{2}(24+2x)\\ &=\sqrt{144-x^2}\times(12+x) \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Shows $h$ or $AB$ correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=12+x & v&=\sqrt{144-x^2}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{144-x^2}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=\sqrt{144-x^2}-\dfrac{x(12+x)}{\sqrt{144-x^2}}$$
Stationary when $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{144-x^2}&=\dfrac{x(12+x)}{\sqrt{144-x^2}}\\ 144-x^2&=x(12+x)\\ 144-x^2&=12x+x^2\\ 2x^2+12x-144&=0\\ x^2+6x-72&=0\\ (x+12)(x-6)&=0\\ x&=-12\text{ or }x=6 \end{aligned}$$
$x$ is a length, so $x>0$ and $x=6$.

Check the nature:

\extable{Ts913_1}

So there is a maximum turning point at $x=6$.

$\therefore$ the trapezium has its maximum area when $x=6$ cm.

496.stem:
Two circles have the same centre $O$. The smaller circle has radius 1 cm, while the larger circle has radius $(1+x)$ cm. The circles enclose a region $QRST$, which is subtended by an angle $\theta$ at $O$, as shaded.

The area of $QRST$ is $A\text{ cm}^2$, where $A$ is a constant and $A>0$.

\exfigure{1628_q31_1}

Let $P$ cm be the perimeter of $QRST$.

figures.cap: concentric circles with shaded annular sector QRST

parts.latex: By finding expressions for the area and perimeter of $QRST$, show that $P(x)=2x+\dfrac{2A}{x}$.
Show that if the perimeter, $P(x)$, is minimised, then $\theta$ must be less than 2.

Area of a sector.reason: Area relation (1) comes from an earlier part; this part only substitutes it, never uses A=½r²θ.

solutions.latex:
The perimeter is two arcs ($l=r\theta$) and two straight edges of length $x$:
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1\theta+(1+x)\theta+2x\\ &= (2+x)\theta+2x\end{aligned}$$
The area is the difference of two sectors ($A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}(1+x)^2\theta-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 1^2\theta\\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\theta\left[1+2x+x^2-1\right]\\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\theta\left(2x+x^2\right)\\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\theta x(2+x) \qquad (1)\end{aligned}$$
From (1):
$$(2+x)\theta=\dfrac{2A}{x}$$
Substituting into $P=(2+x)\theta+2x$:
$$\therefore\ P(x)=2x+\dfrac{2A}{x}$$
criteria: Finds correct expressions for the perimeter and area, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct expression for the perimeter or area, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For a stationary point, $P'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} P' &= 2-\dfrac{2A}{x^2}=0\\ x^2 &= A\\ x &= \sqrt{A} \quad (x>0)\end{aligned}$$
Testing the nature with the second derivative:
$$P''=\dfrac{4A}{x^3}>0 \text{ when } x=\sqrt{A}$$
$\therefore$ This gives a minimum value.

Using (1) with $x=\sqrt{A}$:
$$A=\dfrac{1}{2}\theta\sqrt{A}\left(2+\sqrt{A}\right)$$
$$\theta=\dfrac{2A}{\sqrt{A}\left(2+\sqrt{A}\right)}=\dfrac{2\sqrt{A}}{2+\sqrt{A}}$$
Since $2+\sqrt{A}>\sqrt{A}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \theta &< \dfrac{2\sqrt{A}}{\sqrt{A}}\\ &= 2\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ If $P(x)$ is minimised, $\theta<2$.
criteria: Expresses $\theta$ in terms of $A$, or equivalent merit
Shows $x=\sqrt{A}$ is a minimum, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
If $M$ is the midpoint of $AP$ then $\angle OMA=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. (Do NOT show this)

Find $AM$ in terms of $R$ and $\theta$.
Find an expression, in terms of $v_1$ and $v_2$, for the angle $\theta$ which maximises $t$.
Find the condition on $\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}$ so that the minimum value of $t$ is achieved by only running.

solutions.latex:
In right-angled $\triangle OMA$, $OA=R$:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\theta&=\dfrac{AM}{R} \\ AM&=R\cos\theta \end{aligned}$$

Swim $AP=2AM=2R\cos\theta$. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so $\angle POB=2\theta$ and arc $PB=2R\theta$:
$$t=\dfrac{2R\cos\theta}{v_1}+\dfrac{2R\theta}{v_2}$$
$$\dfrac{dt}{d\theta}=-\dfrac{2R}{v_1}\sin\theta+\dfrac{2R}{v_2}$$
Stationary when $\dfrac{dt}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2R}{v_1}\sin\theta&=\dfrac{2R}{v_2} \\ \sin\theta&=\dfrac{v_1}{v_2} \\ \theta&=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2t}{d\theta^2}=-\dfrac{2R}{v_1}\cos\theta$$
Since $\dfrac{d^2t}{d\theta^2}\le 0$ on the whole domain, $\theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right)$ is a local maximum.

It is the only turning point between the end points, so the maximum cannot occur at an end point.

$\therefore$ $\theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right)$ gives the global maximum.
criteria: Solves $\dfrac{dt}{d\theta}=0$ to get $\theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right)$, or equivalent merit

For the minimum to occur by only running:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi R}{v_2}&<\dfrac{2R}{v_1} \\ \dfrac{v_2}{v_1}&>\dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Find the stationary points:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=24x^2-30x\\ &=6x(4x-5) \end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=\dfrac{5}{4}$, both inside the domain. Evaluate $y$ at the stationary points and the endpoints:

solutions.latex:
Shaded area = sector of the large circle (radius $r$) minus the triangle with two sides $r\sqrt{r}$:

The glass is the two semicircular arcs (together $\pi s$), the two sides of length $w$ and the two dividers of length $s$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2s+2w+\pi s&=200\\ 2w&=200-2s-\pi s\\ w&=100-s\left(\dfrac{2+\pi}{2}\right)\end{aligned}$$

The area is two semicircles of diameter $s$ (one circle) plus the rectangle:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\pi\left(\dfrac{s}{2}\right)^2+w\times s\\ &=\dfrac{\pi s^2}{4}+s\left(100-s\left(\dfrac{\pi+2}{2}\right)\right)\\ &=\dfrac{\pi s^2}{4}+100s-s^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+2}{2}\right)\\ &=100s+\dfrac{\pi s^2}{4}-\dfrac{\pi s^2}{2}-\dfrac{2s^2}{2}\\ &=100s-\dfrac{\pi}{4}s^2-s^2\\ &=100s-s^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}+1\right)\\ A&=100s-s^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)\end{aligned}$$

835.stem:
A light is to be placed over the centre of a circle. The intensity $(I)$ of the light varies as the sine of the angle $(\alpha)$ at which the rays strike the illuminated surface, divided by the square of the distance $(d)$ from the light i.e. $I = \dfrac{k\sin\alpha}{d^2}$ where $k$ is a positive constant.

\exfigure{1359_q33_1}

figures.cap: light at height y above centre O of a circle of radius a; ray of length d to P on the circumference meeting the surface at angle alpha; Radius = a; NOT TO SCALE

parts.latex: Show that: $I = \dfrac{ky}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$
Find the optimal height for a light to be placed over the centre of a circle in order to provide maximum illumination to the circumference. Give your final answer as an exact value.

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle formed by the light, the centre and a point on the circumference, using the sine ratio:
$$\sin\alpha = \dfrac{y}{d}$$
Using Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned} d^2 &= y^2 + a^2 \\ d &= \left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \quad \text{as } d > 0 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute into the given formula:
$$\begin{aligned} I &= \dfrac{k\sin\alpha}{d^2} \\ &= \dfrac{k \times \frac{y}{d}}{d^2} \\ &= \dfrac{ky}{d^3} \\ &= \dfrac{ky}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}} \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Two of: correct $\sin\alpha$, correct $d$, correctly shows $I$ (or 1 error), or equivalent merit
One of the above, or equivalent merit

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dy}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=ky & v&=\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\\ u'&=k & v'&=3y\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dI}{dy} &= \dfrac{k\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} - ky \times 3y\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\left(\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{k\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left[\left(y^2 + a^2\right) - 3y^2\right]}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^3} \\ &= \dfrac{k\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(a^2 - 2y^2\right)}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^3} \\ &= \dfrac{k\left(a^2 - 2y^2\right)}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dI}{dy} = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} k\left(a^2 - 2y^2\right) &= 0 \\ 2y^2 &= a^2 \\ y^2 &= \dfrac{a^2}{2} \\ y &= \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}} \quad \text{as } y > 0 \end{aligned}$$
Only $a^2-2y^2$ decides the sign of $\dfrac{dI}{dy}$. Testing either side:

$\therefore$ The intensity is a maximum when the light is at height $y = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$ m.

A metal container of volume $0.66\pi\ \text{m}^3$ is to be made in the shape of a hollow cylinder of radius r metres and height h metres, closed at the bottom and capped at the top with a hemispherical shell of the same radius. The area of the metal required is $A\ \text{m}^2$.

parts.latex: Given that a sphere with radius $r$ has volume $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ and surface area $4\pi r^2$ and a cylinder of radius $r$ and height $h$ has volume $\pi r^2 h$ and surface area $2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$, show that $A=\dfrac{33\pi}{25r}+\dfrac{5\pi r^2}{3}$.
Hence find the dimensions of such a container that uses the least amount of metal.

solutions.latex:
The volume is a hemisphere plus a cylinder:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3+\pi r^2h&=0.66\pi\\ \dfrac{2}{3}r^3+r^2h&=0.66\\ 2r^3+3r^2h&=\dfrac{99}{50}\\ 3r^2h&=\dfrac{99}{50}-2r^3\\ h&=\dfrac{33}{50r^2}-\dfrac{2r}{3} \end{aligned}$$
The metal is a hemispherical shell, the base circle and the curved side of the cylinder:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times4\pi r^2+\pi r^2+2\pi rh\\ &=2\pi r^2+\pi r^2+2\pi rh\\ &=3\pi r^2+2\pi r\left(\dfrac{33}{50r^2}-\dfrac{2r}{3}\right)\\ &=3\pi r^2+\dfrac{33\pi}{25r}-\dfrac{4\pi r^2}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{33\pi}{25r}+\dfrac{5\pi r^2}{3}\ \text{as required} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds an equation for the surface area in terms of $r$ (eliminating $h$), or equivalent merit
Writes an equation for the volume incorporating the given volume, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{33\pi}{25r}+\dfrac{5\pi r^2}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{33\pi}{25}r^{-1}+\dfrac{5\pi}{3}r^2\\ A'&=-\dfrac{33\pi}{25}r^{-2}+\dfrac{10\pi}{3}r\\ A''&=\dfrac{66\pi}{25}r^{-3}+\dfrac{10\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{10\pi r}{3}-\dfrac{33\pi}{25r^2}&=0\\ \dfrac{10\pi r^3}{3}-\dfrac{33\pi}{25}&=0\\ \dfrac{10\pi r^3}{3}&=\dfrac{33\pi}{25}\\ r^3&=\dfrac{99}{250}\\ \therefore\ r&=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}} \end{aligned}$$
Second derivative test:
$$\begin{aligned} A''&=\dfrac{66\pi}{25}\left(\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}}\right)^{-3}+\dfrac{10\pi}{3}\\ &=10\pi \end{aligned}$$
$A''>0$, so $A$ is a minimum at $r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}}$.

Using $h$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} h&=\dfrac{33}{50r^2}-\dfrac{2r}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{99-100r^3}{150r^2}\\ &=\dfrac{99-100\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{99}{250}}\right)^3}{150\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{99}{250}}\right)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{99-100\left(\frac{99}{250}\right)}{150\left(\frac{99}{250}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}}\\ &=\dfrac{99-\frac{990}{25}}{150}\times\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{297}{750}\times\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\\ &=\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^1\times\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\\ &=\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\\ \therefore\ h&=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The dimensions are $r=h=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}}$ m.

Alternative end of solution, from the volume equation in part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} 2r^3+3r^2h&=1.98\\ h&=\dfrac{1.98-2r^3}{3r^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1.98-2\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{99}{250}}\right)^3}{3\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{99}{250}}\right)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1.98-\frac{99}{125}}{3}\times\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{99}{250}\times\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\\ &=\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\\ \therefore\ h&=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Show that the area, $A$, of the frame and photograph combined is $A=\dfrac{2x^2+12x}{x-4}$.
Find the \underline{exact value of} $x$ such that the area of the frame and photograph combined is a \underline{minimum}. \underline{Show that} your answer gives a minimum area.

solutions.latex:
Let the width of the frame be $y$ cm. The photograph is $(x-4)$ cm by $(y-2)$ cm:
$$\begin{aligned} (x-4)(y-2)&=20\\ y-2&=\dfrac{20}{x-4}\\ y&=\dfrac{20}{x-4}+2\\ &=\dfrac{20+2(x-4)}{x-4}\\ &=\dfrac{20+2x-8}{x-4}\\ &=\dfrac{12+2x}{x-4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A&=x\times y\\ &=x\times\dfrac{12+2x}{x-4}\\ &=\dfrac{12x+2x^2}{x-4}\\ &=\dfrac{2x^2+12x}{x-4} \end{aligned}$$
Or let the width of the photo be $y$, so $(x-4)\times y=20$ and $y=\dfrac{20}{x-4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=x(y+2)\\ &=x\left(\dfrac{20}{x-4}+2\right)\\ &=x\times\dfrac{20+2(x-4)}{x-4}\\ &=x\times\dfrac{20+2x-8}{x-4}\\ &=\dfrac{x(12+2x)}{x-4}\\ &=\dfrac{12x+2x^2}{x-4}\\ &=\dfrac{2x^2+12x}{x-4} \end{aligned}$$

$$x^2-8x-24=0$$

In right-angled triangle $QOR$, with $\tan\theta=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\theta&=\dfrac{QR}{x}\\ QR&=2x\end{aligned}$$

Since $x+y>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}x+y&=\sqrt{25-4x^2}\\ y&=-x+\sqrt{25-4x^2}\end{aligned}$$
The perimeter is $2QR+2RS$:
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2(2x)+2\left(-x+\sqrt{25-4x^2}\right)\\ &=2x+2\sqrt{25-4x^2}\end{aligned}$$

Differentiating (chain rule):
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2x+2\left(25-4x^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ \dfrac{dP}{dx}&=2+2\times\dfrac{1}{2}\left(25-4x^2\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times(-8x)\\ &=2-\dfrac{8x}{\sqrt{25-4x^2}}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}2-\dfrac{8x}{\sqrt{25-4x^2}}&=0\\ \dfrac{8x}{\sqrt{25-4x^2}}&=2\\ 4x&=\sqrt{25-4x^2}\\ 16x^2&=25-4x^2\\ 20x^2&=25\\ x^2&=\dfrac{5}{4}\\ x&=\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\quad(x>0)\end{aligned}$$

A factory produces boxes in the shape of rectangular prisms as shown below.

\exfigure{641_q28_1}

The length, height and width of the box are $l$ cm, $x$ cm and $2x$ cm respectively.

The factory uses $k$ cm$^2$ of sheet metal to make the box, where $k$ is a constant.

parts.latex: Show that $l=\dfrac{k-4x^2}{4x}$, given that the box is open at the top.
Hence find the maximum volume of the box that can be produced from a sheet of metal with an area of 1200 cm$^2$.

solutions.latex:
The box is open at the top, so the sheet metal forms the base and the 4 sides, with total area $k$ cm$^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} k&=2lx+lx+lx+2x^2+2x^2\\ &=4lx+4x^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 4lx&=k-4x^2\\ \therefore\ l&=\dfrac{k-4x^2}{4x} \end{aligned}$$

Let $V$ be the volume of the prism. Using $V=lwh$ and part (a) with $k=1200$:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=2x^2l\\ &=2x^2\left(\dfrac{1200-4x^2}{4x}\right)\\ &=600x-2x^3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} V'&=600-6x^2\\ V''&=-12x \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $V'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6x^2&=600\\ x&=\pm10 \end{aligned}$$
$x>0$ since it represents a side length, so $x=10$.

$V''<0$ when $x=10$, hence the volume is maximised when $x=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} V&=2\times(10)^2\times\left(\dfrac{1200-4\times(10)^2}{4\times(10)}\right)\\ &=4000 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The maximum volume of the box is 4000 cm$^3$.
criteria: Correctly finds and differentiates an expression for the volume in terms of $x$ and finds the value of $x$ that maximises volume, or equivalent merit

The shape below is made of a sector $OAB$ and equilateral triangle $OBC$.

The sector $OAB$ has a radius $r$ cm.

The arc $AB$ subtends an angle $\theta$ radians at $O$.

\exfigure{1371_q33_1}

figures.cap: sector OAB with radius r and angle theta at O, joined along OB to equilateral triangle OBC (tick marks on equal sides)

parts.latex:
Given that the perimeter of the shape is 10 cm, show that

$$A=5r+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}-6}{4}r^2.$$
Hence, determine the maximum area of the shape to the nearest cm$^2$.

solutions.latex:
The perimeter is $OA+\text{arc }AB+BC+CO$, with arc length $r\theta$ and each side of the equilateral triangle equal to $r$:
$$P=3r+r\theta\qquad(1)$$
Substituting $P=10$ into (1):
$$\begin{aligned}3r+r\theta&=10\\r\theta&=10-3r\\\theta&=\dfrac{10-3r}{r}\qquad(2)\end{aligned}$$
Using the sector area $\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ and (2):
$$\begin{aligned}A_1=\text{Area of sector}&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\left(\dfrac{10-3r}{r}\right)\\&=5r-\dfrac{3}{2}r^2\end{aligned}$$
Using $\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ for the equilateral triangle (each angle $60^\circ$):
$$\begin{aligned}A_2=\text{Area of triangle}&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\sin(60^\circ)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}r^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore A&=A_1+A_2\\&=5r-\dfrac{3}{2}r^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}r^2\\&=5r+\dfrac{-6}{4}r^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}r^2\\A&=5r+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}-6}{4}r^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\theta=\dfrac{10-3r}{r}$ and the areas of the sector and the triangle correctly, or equivalent merit

1110.stem:
A water trough is to be made from a 21m long strip of tin by bending up by the angle $\theta$ with a 7m strip at each side, as shown in the diagram. Find the size of angle $\theta$ that would maximize the cross-sectional area, and thus the volume, of the trough.

\exfigure{1373_q39_1}

figures.cap: trough from a strip of tin with 7 m sides bent up at angle theta
solution sketch: trapezium cross-section with sides 7, base 7, top a, height h, overhang x, angle theta

parts.latex: Show that the cross-sectional area is given by $A=49(\sin\theta+\sin\theta\cos\theta)$.
Hence, find the size of angle $\theta$ that would maximise the cross-sectional area of the trough.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1373_q39_s1}

In each right-angled triangle at the sides (hypotenuse $7$), using the sine and cosine ratios:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin\theta&=\dfrac{h}{7} & h&=7\sin\theta\\\cos\theta&=\dfrac{x}{7} & x&=7\cos\theta\end{aligned}$$
The cross-section is a trapezium with parallel sides $7$ and $7+2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}h(a+b)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(7\sin\theta)(7+7+2x)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(7\sin\theta)\big(14+2(7\cos\theta)\big)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(7\sin\theta)(14+14\cos\theta)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(7\sin\theta)\,14(1+\cos\theta)\\&=49\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)\\&=49(\sin\theta+\sin\theta\cos\theta)\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: All steps must be shown properly.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin\theta & v&=\cos\theta\\ u'&=\cos\theta & v'&=-\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=49(\sin\theta+\sin\theta\cos\theta)\\A'&=49(\cos\theta+\cos\theta\cos\theta-\sin\theta\sin\theta)\\&=49(\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)\\A''&=49(-\sin\theta-2\cos\theta\sin\theta-2\sin\theta\cos\theta)\\&=49(-\sin\theta-4\sin\theta\cos\theta)\end{aligned}$$
For a maximum or minimum, $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta&=0\\\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta-(1-\cos^2\theta)&=0\\2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1&=0\\2\cos^2\theta+2\cos\theta-\cos\theta-1&=0\\2\cos\theta(\cos\theta+1)-(\cos\theta+1)&=0\\(2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos\theta=-1$.

$\theta$ must be acute, so $\theta\ne\pi$ and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

Testing with the second derivative:
$$\begin{aligned}A''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=49\left(-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}-4\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\\&=49\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-4\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right)\\&=49\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\\&=-\dfrac{147\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&<0\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the cross-sectional area is a maximum when $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

A drain is made by folding up a rectangular sheet of metal, with cross- sectional length of 6 m, to form a cross-sectional area in the shape of an isosceles trapezium, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1375_q35_1}

figures.cap: cross-section of drain: isosceles trapezium, base and sloping sides 2 m each (tick marks), sides inclined at angle theta to the horizontal
solution sketch: drain diagram annotated: sloping sides 2, base 2, height 2 sin theta, horizontal 2 cos theta

parts.latex:
Show that the area of the trapezoidal cross section of the drain can be expressed as

$A=\sin\vartheta(4+4\cos\vartheta)$ where $\vartheta$ is the angle in radians that the metal sheet is bent to form the drain.
Find the angle $\vartheta$ that maximizes the cross-sectional area.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1375_q35_s1}

From the diagram, the base and each sloping side are $2$ m, so the height is $2\sin\theta$ and each side adds $2\cos\theta$ to the top width.

Using the area of a trapezium, $A=\dfrac{1}{2}h(a+b)$ (or a rectangle plus two triangles):
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}(2\sin\theta)(2+2+4\cos\theta)\\&=\sin\theta(4+4\cos\theta)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the height $2\sin\theta$ and the width $2\cos\theta$ (may be shown on the diagram), or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: The area must be explicitly shown.

solutions.latex:
Expanding the area from part (i):
$$A=4\sin\theta+4\sin\theta\cos\theta$$
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, on $4\sin\theta\cos\theta$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=4\sin\theta & v&=\cos\theta\\u'&=4\cos\theta & v'&=-\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}&=4\cos\theta+4\sin\theta(-\sin\theta)+4\cos\theta\cos\theta\\&=4\cos\theta-4(1-\cos^2\theta)+4\cos^2\theta\\&=8\cos^2\theta+4\cos\theta-4\end{aligned}$$
For a maximum or minimum, $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}4(2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1)&=0\\(2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos\theta=-1$.

$\theta$ is an angle in a right-angled triangle, so $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ only:
$$\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
Testing with the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}=16\cos\theta(-\sin\theta)-4\sin\theta$$
At $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}&=16\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\times\left(-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-4\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\&=16\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-4\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=-4\sqrt{3}-2\sqrt{3}\\&=-6\sqrt{3}<0\end{aligned}$$
So the area is a maximum when $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

$\therefore$ the angle that maximises the area is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ (or $60^\circ$).

parts.latex: A 40-centimetre length of wire is cut into three pieces. Two pieces are bent to form two congruent circles and the final piece is bent to form a square.
If the radius of each congruent circle is $r$ centimetres, show that the total area of the three shapes is given by $A=(10-\pi r)^2+2\pi r^2$
Hence, find the length of the side of the square and the value of $r$ that will minimise the total area of the three shapes.

Chain rule.reason: (10 - pi r)^2 could be expanded first; chain rule is one valid method.

Second derivative.reason: Nature of the minimum may be shown by any method (e.g. table of slopes).

solutions.latex:
Let the side length of the square be $x$. The wire forms two circles (circumference $2\pi r$ each) and the square (perimeter $4x$):
$$\begin{aligned}40&=2\pi r+2\pi r+4x\\ 40&=4\pi r+4x\\ 10&=\pi r+x\\ x&=10-\pi r\end{aligned}$$
The total area is two circles ($\pi r^2$ each) and the square ($x^2$):
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ A&=2\pi r^2+(10-\pi r)^2\\ &=(10-\pi r)^2+2\pi r^2\text{ as required}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes $40=2\pi r+2\pi r+4x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiating (chain rule on $(10-\pi r)^2$):
$$\begin{aligned}A&=(10-\pi r)^2+2\pi r^2\\ \dfrac{dA}{dr}&=2(10-\pi r)\times(-\pi)+4\pi r\\ &=-20\pi+2\pi^2r+4\pi r\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points when $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=-20\pi+2\pi^2r+4\pi r\\ 20\pi&=2\pi^2r+4\pi r\\ 10&=\pi r+2r\\ 10&=r(\pi+2)\\ r&=\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}\end{aligned}$$
Checking the nature using $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}$:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=2\pi^2+4\pi>0\text{ for all }r$$
$\therefore\ A$ is always concave up, so there is a minimum at $r=\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}$.

At $r=\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=10-\pi\left(\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{10(\pi+2)-10\pi}{\pi+2}\\ &=\dfrac{20}{\pi+2}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the area is minimised when $r=\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}$ cm and the side of the square is $\dfrac{20}{\pi+2}$ cm.
criteria: Finds $r=\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}$ and verifies the minimum, or equivalent merit

1214.stem: May has a mango orchard with 20 trees that each produce 400 mangoes per year. For every additional tree that May plants in the orchard, the output of every tree decreases by 10 mangoes per year.

parts.latex: Show that the number of mangoes, $M$, produced by May’s orchard each year is given by $M=-10x^2+200x+8000$ where $x$ is the number of additional trees planted.
Hence find the number of additional trees May should plant in order to maximise the number of mangoes grown each year.

solutions.latex:
Number of trees $=20+x$; mangoes per tree $=400-10x$.
$$\begin{aligned} M &= (20+x)(400-10x) \\ &= 8000-200x+400x-10x^2 \\ &= -10x^2+200x+8000 \end{aligned}$$

$$M'=-20x+200$$
Stationary points when $M'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -20x+200 \\ 20x &= 200 \\ x &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
$M''=-20<0$ for all $x$, so there is a local maximum at $x=10$.

$\therefore$ May should plant 10 more trees.

1261.stem:
Feifei ($F$) and Airi ($A$) are on opposing sides of a river bank. Feifei can run at a rate of 7km/hr and row at a rate of 5km/hr. The river bank is 800 metres wide and there would be 2.5 kilometres between Feifei and Airi if they were on the same side of the shore. Feifei wishes to meet Airi. Let $x$ be the distance from directly opposite from Feifei's starting point to her exit point ($E$) from the water and let $t$ be the total time taken for Feifei to meet Airi.

\exfigure{572_q25_1}

figures.cap: river 800 m wide between two shores; F on lower shore, E on upper shore a distance x from the point opposite F, A on upper shore, 2.5 km marked from A to the point opposite F

parts.latex: Show that the time ($t$) taken for Feifei to row and then run to Airi can be given by the equation $t=\dfrac{2.5-x}{7}+\dfrac{\sqrt{0.64+x^2}}{5}$.
Hence, or otherwise, find how far Feifei must run along the shore in order to minimise the time taken to reach Airi. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

solutions.latex:
Let $d$ km be Feifei's rowing distance. The river is $800\text{ m}=0.8\text{ km}$ wide, so by Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle with legs $0.8$ and $x$:
$$\begin{aligned}d^2&=0.8^2+x^2\\&=0.64+x^2\\d&=\sqrt{0.64+x^2}\end{aligned}$$
She rows $d$ km at $5$ km/h and runs $(2.5-x)$ km at $7$ km/h. Using time $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$:
$$t=\dfrac{2.5-x}{7}+\dfrac{\sqrt{0.64+x^2}}{5}$$

Writing the square root as a power and differentiating (chain rule):

The figure below shows the design of coffee jar with a lid sitting directly on top.

\exfigure{317_q30_1}

The jar is in the shape of a right circular cylinder of radius $x\text{ cm}$. It is fitted with a lid of height $2\text{ cm}$, which fits tightly on the top of the jar, so it may be assumed that it has the same radius as the jar. The total metal used to make the jar and its lid is $190\pi\text{ cm}^2$.

The metal is the curved surfaces of the jar (height $h$) and the lid (height 2), plus the base and the top of the lid:
$$\begin{aligned}2\pi x(h+2)+2(\pi x^2)&=190\pi\\2x(h+2)+2x^2&=190\\x(h+2)+x^2&=95\\xh+2x+x^2&=95\\xh&=95-2x-x^2\end{aligned}$$
Using the cylinder volume $V=\pi r^2h$ with $r=x$:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\pi x^2h\\&=\pi x(xh)\\&=\pi x(95-2x-x^2)\\&=\pi(95x-2x^2-x^3)\end{aligned}$$

When $x=5$, $\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=-34\pi<0$

$\therefore$ maximum occurs when $x=5$

Volume of a pyramid, $V=\dfrac{1}{3}Ah$, with base $3b\times b$ and height $OM=x$:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\dfrac{1}{3}Ah\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}(3b\times b)x\\ &=b^2x\end{aligned}$$
$DB$ is a diagonal of the rectangular base, so by Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle DAB$:
$$\begin{aligned}DB^2&=b^2+(3b)^2\\ DB&=\sqrt{b^2+9b^2}\\ &=\sqrt{10b^2}\end{aligned}$$
Equating with $DB=2\sqrt{r^2-x^2}$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{10b^2}&=2\sqrt{r^2-x^2}\\ 10b^2&=4(r^2-x^2)\\ b^2&=\dfrac{4(r^2-x^2)}{10}\end{aligned}$$
Substituting into $V=b^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\dfrac{2}{5}(r^2-x^2)x\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5}x(r^2-x^2)\end{aligned}$$

A factory produces boxes in the shape of an open rectangular prism (without a lid).

\exfigure{323_q23_1}

The length, height and width of the box are $l$ cm, $x$ cm and $2x$ cm respectively.

The factory uses $k \text{ cm}^2$ of sheet metal to make the box, where $k$ is a constant.

figures.cap: open rectangular box with length l, height x and width 2x

parts.latex: Show that $l = \dfrac{k - 4x^2}{4x}$.
Hence, find the maximum volume of the box that can be produced from a sheet of metal with an area of $1200 \text{ cm}^2$.

solutions.latex:
The open box has a base $l\times 2x$, two sides $l\times x$ and two ends $2x\times x$:
$$\begin{aligned} k&=2lx+2lx+2(2x^2)\\ k&=4lx+4x^2\\ 4lx&=k-4x^2\\ l&=\dfrac{k-4x^2}{4x} \end{aligned}$$

Volume $=$ length $\times$ width $\times$ height, with $l$ from part (a) and $k=1200$:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=2x^2l\\ &=2x^2\left(\dfrac{1200-4x^2}{4x}\right)\\ &=600x-2x^3\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $V'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}V'&=600-6x^2\\ 600-6x^2&=0\\ 6x^2&=600\\ x^2&=100\\ x&=\pm 10\end{aligned}$$
Nature, using $V''=-12x$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=10: & V''&=-120<0 &&\text{maximum}\\ x&=-10: & V''&=120>0 &&\text{minimum}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \text{max volume}&=2\times 10^2\times\dfrac{1200-4(10)^2}{40}\\ &=4000 \text{ cm}^3\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $x=10$ and shows it gives a maximum, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Show that the area, $A$, of the quadrilateral $OMPN$ is given by

$A=5\sin\theta+10\cos\theta$.
Find the value of $\tan\theta$ which gives the maximum area $A$.
Hence find the coordinates of point $P$ in surd form when $A$ is maximum

solutions.latex:
Using area $=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ in $\triangle OMP$, with $OP=5$ (radius) and $OM=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of }\triangle OMP&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times5\times\sin\theta\\ &=5\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
In $\triangle ONP$, $OP=5$, $ON=4$ and $\angle NOP=\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of }\triangle ONP&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times4\times5\times\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)\\ &=10\cos\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore A&=\text{Area of }\triangle OMP+\text{Area of }\triangle ONP\\ &=5\sin\theta+10\cos\theta\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one or both areas of the triangles, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: one or both areas of triangles

solutions.latex:
A maximum may occur where $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}&=5\cos\theta-10\sin\theta\\ 5\cos\theta-10\sin\theta&=0\\ 10\sin\theta&=5\cos\theta\\ \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}&=\dfrac{5}{10}=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \tan\theta&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
With $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ (right-angled triangle with sides $1$, $2$, $\sqrt{5}$):
$$\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\quad \cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}&=-5\sin\theta-10\cos\theta\\ &=-5\sin\left(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-10\cos\left(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=-5\times\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}-10\times\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}<0\end{aligned}$$
Concave down, so $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ gives the maximum area.

For maximum area, $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$, so $\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$.

$P$ is on the circle of radius $5$, so $\dfrac{x}{5}=\cos\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=5\times\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\\ &=2\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}$$
From $x^2+y^2=25$, with $y>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\sqrt{25-x^2}\\ &=\sqrt{25-20}\\ &=\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore P\left(2\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}\right)$

1526.stem:
A truck travels between two towns. The distance between the towns is $B$ km.

The trucker has the following costs:

The hourly fuel costs are proportional to the square of the speed.

The hourly fuel cost is \$2000 when the speed is 40 km/h.

All other costs are \$4800 per hour. Let $x$ be the speed in km/h and $C$ be the total cost.

parts.latex: Show that $C=B\left(\dfrac{5}{4}x+\dfrac{4800}{x}\right)$.
What is the most economical speed?

solutions.latex:
The hourly fuel cost is proportional to $x^2$, so it is $kx^2$.

When $x=40$ the hourly fuel cost is $\$2000$:

$$\begin{aligned} 2000 &= k\times 40^2 \\ k &= \dfrac{2000}{1600} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{4} \end{aligned}$$

Hourly cost $=$ fuel cost $+$ other costs:

$$\text{Hourly cost}=\dfrac{5}{4}x^2+4800$$

Since speed $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$, the time for the trip is $\dfrac{B}{x}$ hours.

$$\begin{aligned} C &= \left(\dfrac{5}{4}x^2+4800\right)\times\dfrac{B}{x} \\ &= B\left(\dfrac{5}{4}x+\dfrac{4800}{x}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the hourly cost $\dfrac{5}{4}x^2+4800$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The most economical speed minimises $C$.

$$\begin{aligned} C &= B\left(\dfrac{5}{4}x+\dfrac{4800}{x}\right) \\ \dfrac{dC}{dx} &= B\left(\dfrac{5}{4}-\dfrac{4800}{x^2}\right) \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dC}{dx}=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5}{4}-\dfrac{4800}{x^2} &= 0 \\ 5x^2 &= 4800\times 4 \\ x^2 &= 3840 \\ x &= \pm 61.96773\ldots \end{aligned}$$

Speed is positive, so $x=\sqrt{3840}\approx 61.97$.

Test the nature with the second derivative:

$$\dfrac{d^2C}{dx^2}=B\times\dfrac{9600}{x^3}$$

At $x=61.97$, $\dfrac{d^2C}{dx^2}>0$ since $B>0$ (a distance).

So the cost is a minimum.

$$\therefore\ \text{the most economical speed is } x=\sqrt{3840}\approx 61.97 \text{ km/h}$$
criteria: Differentiates correctly and equates to zero, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correct differentiation and equating to zero

1564.stem:
A homeowner intends to construct a rectangular pool in their backyard with a length of $x$ m and a width of $y$ m.

The depth will steadily increase from 1 m to $\dfrac{2x}{3}$ m, as seen in the diagram below.

The homeowner wishes to put tiles around the edge of the surface of the pool, and has enough to tile a perimeter of 27 m.

\exfigure{347_q32_1}

figures.cap: rectangular pool, length x m, width y m, depth increasing from 1 m at one end to 2x/3 m at the other

parts.latex: Show that the volume of the pool is $V(x)=-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+4x^2+\dfrac{27}{4}x$.
Hence, find the maximum volume of the pool.

Confirm that the volume in part (b) is a maximum.

Include reasoning and calculations in your response.

solutions.latex:
From the diagram, the volume is the average depth times the length and width:

$$V=\dfrac{x}{2}\left(1+\dfrac{2x}{3}\right)y \qquad (1)$$

The perimeter is $27$ m:

$$\begin{aligned} 2x+2y &= 27 \\ y &= \dfrac{27}{2}-x \qquad (2) \end{aligned}$$

Substitute (2) into (1):

$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{x}{2}\left(1+\dfrac{2x}{3}\right)\left(\dfrac{27}{2}-x\right) \\ &= \dfrac{x}{2}\left(\dfrac{27}{2}-x+9x-\dfrac{2x^2}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{x}{2}\left(\dfrac{27}{2}+8x-\dfrac{2x^2}{3}\right) \\ V(x) &= -\dfrac{x^3}{3}+4x^2+\dfrac{27}{4}x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly substitutes equation (2) into equation (1), or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correctly substitutes eq. 2 into eq. 1 or equivalent

solutions.latex:
The maximum occurs where $V'(x)=0$:

$$V'(x)=-x^2+8x+\dfrac{27}{4}$$

$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= x^2-8x-\dfrac{27}{4} \\ x &= \dfrac{8\pm\sqrt{64-4(1)\left(-\frac{27}{4}\right)}}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{8\pm\sqrt{91}}{2} \\ &\approx 8.7697 \text{ or } -0.77 \end{aligned}$$

Length is positive, so ignore the negative value.

$$\begin{aligned} V(8.7697) &= -\dfrac{(8.7697)^3}{3}+4(8.7697)^2+\dfrac{27}{4}(8.7697) \\ &= 142\text{ m}^3 \text{ (3 significant figures)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly solves the quadratic, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the handwritten substitution omitted the minus sign on the $\frac{x^3}{3}$ term; it should read $-\frac{x^3}{3}$ (final value 142 unchanged).

solutions.latex:
$$V''(x)=-2x+8$$

$$V''(8.7697)\approx -9.5$$

$$\begin{aligned} V'(8.7697) &= 0 &&\text{stationary point} \\ V''(8.7697) &< 0 &&\text{concave down} \end{aligned}$$

So the stationary point is a local maximum.

The domain is $0<x<13.5$ because the perimeter is $27$ m, and $V(0)=V(13.5)=0$.

So the local maximum is the maximum volume.

parts.latex:
A wire of length 28 m is to be cut into two pieces. One of the pieces is to be made into a square and the other into a circle.

Let $r$ metres be the radius of the circle and $x$ metres be the length of each side of the square.

The combined perimeter is given as $2\pi r+4x=28$ and the combined area, $A$, is given by:

$$A=\pi\left(\dfrac{14-2x}{\pi}\right)^2+x^2\ \ (\textbf{DO NOT PROVE THIS})$$

What should be the lengths of each piece so that the combined area of the circle and the square is minimum? Leave your answer in simplest exact form.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate the given area to find the stationary point:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\pi\left(\dfrac{14-2x}{\pi}\right)^2+x^2\\A'&=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cdot2(14-2x)(-2)+2x\\&=-\dfrac{8}{\pi}(7-x)+2x\\A''&=\dfrac{8}{\pi}+2\end{aligned}$$
Set $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{8}{\pi}(7-x)+2x&=0\\-\dfrac{56}{\pi}+\dfrac{8x}{\pi}+2x&=0\\-56+8x+2\pi x&=0\\2x(4+\pi)&=56\\x&=\dfrac{28}{4+\pi}\end{aligned}$$
$A''=\dfrac{8}{\pi}+2>0$ for all $x$ (concave up), so $x=\dfrac{28}{4+\pi}$ gives a minimum.

The square has perimeter $4x$ and the circle has the rest of the wire, so the lengths of the two pieces are
$$4x=\dfrac{112}{4+\pi}\text{ m}$$
and
$$\begin{aligned}28-4x&=28-\dfrac{112}{4+\pi}\\&=\dfrac{28\pi}{4+\pi}\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantially correct solution, or equivalent merit
Some correct working towards the correct solution, or equivalent merit

where $t$ is the time in months. It is known that the initial population of birds is 34.

parts.latex: You are given $\int_0^4e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}\,dt\approx22.26$, show that $P=218$ to the nearest integer at $t=4$.

A coal mine was recently built near the wildlife preserve and pollution from the mine affects the population of the birds from $t=4$ onwards. Kevin who works as an environmentalist, models that the population size of the birds can then be approximated by $P=Ate^{-0.05t}-100,\ (t\ge4)$.

Using part (a), show that $A=97$.
Determine the maximum population size, leave your answer as an integer.
The population size of the birds is modelled by $P=97te^{-0.05t}-100$, for $t\ge4$, as shown and derived in part (b). Make $e^{0.05t}$ the subject of this equation.

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=9e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}-2t$, the change in the population from $t=0$ to $t=4$ is
$$\begin{aligned}P(4)-P(0)&=\int_0^4\left(9e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}-2t\right)dt\\&=9\int_0^4e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}\,dt-\int_0^42t\,dt\end{aligned}$$
With $P(0)=34$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(4)&=9\int_0^4e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}\,dt-\Big[t^2\Big]_0^4+P(0)\\&=9(22.26)-16+34\\&=218.34\ldots\\&\approx218\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $P=218$ when $t=4$. Substitute into $P=Ate^{-0.05t}-100$:
$$\begin{aligned}218&=A(4)e^{-0.05\times4}-100\\318&=4Ae^{-0.2}\\A&=\dfrac{318}{4e^{-0.2}}\\&=97.10151927\ldots\\&\approx97\end{aligned}$$

Differentiate using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=t & v&=e^{-0.05t}\\u'&=1 & v'&=-0.05e^{-0.05t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}P&=97te^{-0.05t}-100\\P'&=97\left(1\times e^{-0.05t}-0.05te^{-0.05t}\right)\\&=97e^{-0.05t}(1-0.05t)\end{aligned}$$

The diagram below shows a large bio-diversity precinct the council is planning to build inside a large park. $OAB$ is a sector with centre $O$, and radius $x$ kilometres. Arc $AB$ subtends an angle of $\theta$ radians at $O$. The equilateral triangle $BCO$ adjoins the sector.

\exfigure{361_q36_1}

figures.cap: sector OAB with radius x and angle theta at O, joined along OB to equilateral triangle BCO with sides x

parts.latex:
The perimeter of the precinct as shown in the diagram is given to be $\left(12-2\sqrt{3}\right)$ kilometres.

Calculate the maximum area of the precinct $(OABC)$. Leave your answer in exact form.

solutions.latex:
The perimeter is $OA+\text{arc }AB+BC+CO$, where $OA=BC=CO=x$ (radius, and equilateral triangle $BCO$), so
$$\text{Arc } AB=12-2\sqrt{3}-3x$$
Arc length is $x\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} x\theta&=12-2\sqrt{3}-3x \\ \theta&=\dfrac{12}{x}-\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{x}-3 \end{aligned}$$
Triangle $BCO$ is equilateral, so $\angle BOC=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area } \triangle OBC&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times x^2\times\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\times x^2\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}x^2}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\text{Area of sector}=\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\theta=\dfrac{x^2}{2}\theta$$
Area of the precinct is the area of the triangle plus the area of the sector:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}x^2}{4}+\dfrac{x^2}{2}\left(\dfrac{12}{x}-\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{x}-3\right) \\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}x^2}{4}+6x-\sqrt{3}x-\dfrac{3x^2}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{(\sqrt{3}-6)x^2}{4}+(6-\sqrt{3})x \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=\dfrac{(\sqrt{3}-6)x}{2}+(6-\sqrt{3})$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{(\sqrt{3}-6)x}{2}+(6-\sqrt{3})&=0 \\ x&=\dfrac{-2(6-\sqrt{3})}{\sqrt{3}-6} \\ &=\dfrac{2(\sqrt{3}-6)}{\sqrt{3}-6} \\ &=2 \end{aligned}$$
Since $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}-6}{2}<0$, $x=2$ gives a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{4(\sqrt{3}-6)}{4}+2(6-\sqrt{3}) \\ &=6-\sqrt{3} \text{ km}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the expression for $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct expression for the total area of the precinct, or equivalent merit

1682.stem:
A $100$ cm length of wire is cut into two pieces at point P, as shown in the diagram, where $x$ is the length of one of the two pieces of wire.

\exfigure{1601_q3_2}

figures.cap: 100 cm wire with point P; first piece of length x

parts.latex:
The piece that is length $x$ is used to form a circle and the other is used to form a square. Show that the total area of the circle and square can be given by:

$$A=\dfrac{x^2}{4\pi}+\dfrac{(100-x)^2}{16}$$
At what length should $x$ be cut to minimise the total area of the circle and square? Give your answer to the nearest centimetre.

solutions.latex:
The piece of length $x$ is the circumference of the circle:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\pi r&=x \\ r&=\dfrac{x}{2\pi} \end{aligned}$$
The other piece has length $100-x$ and is the perimeter of the square, so each side is $\dfrac{100-x}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{circle}}&=\pi\left(\dfrac{x}{2\pi}\right)^2 \\ A_{\text{square}}&=\left(\dfrac{100-x}{4}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total area}&=\dfrac{\pi x^2}{4\pi^2}+\left(\dfrac{100-x}{4}\right)^2 \\ &=\dfrac{x^2}{4\pi}+\dfrac{(100-x)^2}{16} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the area of the circle or the area of the square, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{x^2}{4\pi}+\dfrac{(100-x)^2}{16} \\ A'&=\dfrac{2x}{4\pi}-\dfrac{2(100-x)}{16} \\ &=\dfrac{x}{2\pi}-\dfrac{100-x}{8} \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{2\pi}-\dfrac{100-x}{8}&=0 \\ \dfrac{4x-\pi(100-x)}{8\pi}&=0 \\ 4x-100\pi+\pi x&=0 \\ x(4+\pi)&=100\pi \\ x&=\dfrac{100\pi}{4+\pi} \\ &=43.99\ldots \\ &\approx44 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
Check that $44$ cm gives a minimum:
$$\begin{aligned} A''&=\dfrac{1}{2\pi}+\dfrac{1}{8} \\ &=0.28\ldots \\ &>0 \text{ for all } x \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $44$ cm is a minimum, so the wire should be cut at $44$ cm to minimise the total area of the square and the circle.

parts.latex:
An open-topped fish tank of volume $90\,\text{m}^3$ is to be made in the shape of a rectangular prism of length $2x$ metres, width $x$ metres, and height $h$ metres. Materials cost \$15 per square metre for the base of the tank and \$20 per square metre for the sides of the tank.

Show that the total cost \$$C$ of making the fish tank is given by

$$C=30x^2+\dfrac{5\,400}{x}$$

and hence find the dimensions of the fish tank with the least total cost.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{373_q25_s1}

The base is $2x$ by $x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of base}&=2x\times x=2x^2 \\ \text{Cost of base}&=15\times2x^2=\$30x^2 \end{aligned}$$
The volume is $90\text{ m}^3$:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=h\times2x\times x \\ 90&=2x^2h \\ h&=\dfrac{45}{x^2} \end{aligned}$$
The four sides have total area
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of sides}&=2\times h\times2x+2\times x\times h \\ &=4xh+2xh \\ &=6xh \\ &=6x\times\dfrac{45}{x^2} \\ &=\dfrac{270}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cost of sides}&=20\times\dfrac{270}{x} \\ &=\$\dfrac{5400}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore C=30x^2+\dfrac{5400}{x}$$
To minimise the cost, let $\dfrac{dC}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dC}{dx}&=60x-\dfrac{5400}{x^2}=0 \\ 60x&=\dfrac{5400}{x^2} \\ x^3&=90 \\ x&=\sqrt[3]{90} \end{aligned}$$
Check that $x=\sqrt[3]{90}$ is a minimum:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2C}{dx^2}&=60+\dfrac{10800}{x^3} \\ &=60+\dfrac{10800}{90} &&(x^3=90) \\ &=180>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the cost is least when $x=\sqrt[3]{90}$, and the dimensions of the tank are
$$\begin{aligned} \text{length}&=2\sqrt[3]{90} \text{ m} \\ \text{width}&=\sqrt[3]{90} \text{ m} \\ \text{height}&=\dfrac{45}{\left(\sqrt[3]{90}\right)^2}=\dfrac{45}{90^{\frac{2}{3}}} \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows the total cost, or equivalent merit
Finds the cost of the sides, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:

Show that

$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=\sqrt{9-x^2}-\dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}$$
Hence find the maximum area of the rectangle.

solutions.latex:
Since $x^2+y^2=9$:
$$\begin{aligned} y^2 &= 9-x^2 \\ y &= \sqrt{9-x^2} &&(y\text{ is a length, so positive}) \end{aligned}$$
The area of the rectangle is length times width:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= xy \\ &= x\sqrt{9-x^2} \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=(9-x^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2}(9-x^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\cdot(-2x)=-\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\end{aligned}$$
where $v'$ is found by the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= u'v+uv' \\ &= 1\cdot\sqrt{9-x^2}+x\cdot\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{9-x^2}} \\ &= \sqrt{9-x^2}-\dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}} \end{aligned}$$

For a maximum or minimum, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$ (using part (b)):
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{9-x^2}-\dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}} &= 0 \\ 9-x^2-x^2 &= 0 &&(\text{multiply by }\sqrt{9-x^2}) \\ 9-2x^2 &= 0 \\ x^2 &= \dfrac{9}{2} \\ x &= \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} &&(x\text{ is a length, so positive}) \\ &= \dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature of the stationary point with the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ either side of $x=\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$:

\extable{Ts2638_1}

The gradient changes from positive to negative, so $A$ is a maximum when $x=\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$ cm.
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\max} &= x\sqrt{9-x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{9-\dfrac{9}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{9}{2}\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$

An open topped fish tank of volume 30 m$^3$ is to be made in the shape of a rectangular prism with length $3x$ metres, width $x$ metres and height $h$ metres.

Materials cost \$20 per square metre for the base of the tank and \$35 per square metre for the sides of the tank.

Show that the total cost \$$C$ of making the fish tank is given by

$$C=60x^2+\dfrac{2800}{x}$$
Hence find the dimensions of such a tank with the least total cost. Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The volume is $30$ m$^3$, so
$$\begin{aligned} 3x\cdot x\cdot h &= 30 \\ h &= \dfrac{10}{x^2} \end{aligned}$$
The base has area $3x\cdot x=3x^2$ and the four sides (open top) have area $2(3x\cdot h)+2(x\cdot h)=8xh$.
$$\begin{aligned} C &= 20\times3x^2+35\times8xh \\ &= 60x^2+280x\times\dfrac{10}{x^2} \\ &= 60x^2+\dfrac{2800}{x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the area of the base and of the sides and substitutes into the cost, or equivalent merit

Minimise $C=60x^2+2800x^{-1}$ for $x>0$.

Stationary points: $\dfrac{dC}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 120x &= \dfrac{2800}{x^2} \\ x^3 &= \dfrac{70}{3} \\ x &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{70}{3}}\approx2.858 \end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{d^2C}{dx^2}=120+\dfrac{5600}{x^3}>0 \text{ for } x>0$$
so the stationary point is a minimum.

The width is $x\approx2.858$ m, the length is $3x\approx8.573$ m, and the height is $h=\dfrac{10}{x^2}\approx1.225$ m.

1953.stem:
Consider the following diagram with the cone inscribed in a sphere.

\exfigure{402_q29_1}

figures.cap: cone ABC inscribed in a sphere with centre O, radius R, base radius r, height h
solution sketch: cone-in-sphere diagram with OA = R and OD = h - R marked

parts.latex: If $r$ is the radius of the cone show that $r^2=2hR-h^2$.
Show that the volume of the cone that can be inscribed in a sphere of radius $R$ is given by $V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(2h^2R-h^3\right)$ where $h$ is the height of the inscribed cone.
Show that the volume of the largest cone is $\dfrac{8}{27}$ of the volume of the sphere.

solutions.latex:
The volume of a cone is $V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$. Substitute $r^2=2hR-h^2$ from part (i):
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(2hR-h^2\right)h\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(2h^2R-h^3\right)\end{aligned}$$

Let $V_C=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(2h^2R-h^3\right)$ be the volume of the cone and $V_S=\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3$ the volume of the sphere. Differentiate with respect to $h$:
$$\dfrac{dV_C}{dh}=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(4Rh-3h^2\right),\qquad\dfrac{d^2V_C}{dh^2}=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(4R-6h\right)$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dV_C}{dh}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}4Rh-3h^2&=0\\ h\left(4R-3h\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$h=0$ is rejected since $h>0$, so $h=\dfrac{4R}{3}$.

Second derivative test at $h=\dfrac{4R}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2V_C}{dh^2}&=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(4R-6\cdot\dfrac{4R}{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi(4R-8R)\\ &=-\dfrac{4\pi R}{3}\end{aligned}$$
This is negative since $R>0$, so $h=\dfrac{4R}{3}$ gives a maximum.

The maximum volume of the cone is
$$\begin{aligned}V_C&=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(2R\left(\dfrac{4R}{3}\right)^2-\left(\dfrac{4R}{3}\right)^3\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(\dfrac{32R^3}{9}-\dfrac{64R^3}{27}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\cdot\dfrac{96R^3-64R^3}{27}\\ &=\dfrac{32\pi R^3}{81}\end{aligned}$$
Compare with the sphere:
$$\dfrac{V_C}{V_S}=\dfrac{32\pi R^3}{81}\cdot\dfrac{3}{4\pi R^3}=\dfrac{8}{27}$$
Therefore the volume of the largest cone is $\dfrac{8}{27}$ of the volume of the sphere.

parts.latex:
The diagram below shows a shaded sector in a circle with radius $r$ and centre $O$.

The sector subtends an angle of $\theta$ at the centre of the circle.

The area of the sector is $49\ \text{cm}^2$.

\exfigure{162_q14_2}

Show that $\theta=\dfrac{98}{r^2}$ and hence show that the minimum perimeter of the sector will occur when the arc length of the sector is equal to the diameter of the circle.

solutions.latex:
The sector area is $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta=49$.
$$\begin{aligned}r^2\theta&=98\\\theta&=\dfrac{98}{r^2}\end{aligned}$$
The perimeter is two radii plus the arc $r\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2r+r\theta\\&=2r+r\cdot\dfrac{98}{r^2}\\&=2r+98r^{-1}\\\dfrac{dP}{dr}&=2-98r^{-2}\\&=2-\dfrac{98}{r^2}\end{aligned}$$
A stationary point occurs when $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}2-\dfrac{98}{r^2}&=0\\2r^2&=98\\r^2&=49\end{aligned}$$
Since $r>0$, $r=7$.

Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}=196r^{-3}=\dfrac{196}{r^3}$$
When $r=7$, $\dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}=\dfrac{196}{343}=\dfrac{4}{7}>0$, so $P$ is a minimum.

Then the arc length is
$$r\theta=7\times\dfrac{98}{7^2}=14=2\times 7.$$
$\therefore$ the perimeter is a minimum when the arc length equals the diameter of the circle.

2321.stem:
The cross section of a treasure chest is in the shape of a rectangle and a semicircle. The total perimeter of the cross section is 250 cm.

\exfigure{292_q26_1}

figures.cap: rectangle of width x and height y topped by a semicircle

parts.latex:
Show that the area of the of the cross section is given by:

$$A=125x-x^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{8}\right).$$
Find the maximum area of the cross-section of the treasure chest giving your answer correct to one decimal place.

solutions.latex:
The perimeter is the base $x$, two sides $y$, and a semicircular arc of radius $\dfrac{x}{2}$, length $\dfrac{1}{2}\pi x$.
$$\begin{aligned}250&=2y+x+\dfrac{1}{2}\pi x\\2y&=250-\dfrac{2x+\pi x}{2}\\y&=125-\dfrac{2x+\pi x}{4}\end{aligned}$$
The area is a rectangle plus a semicircle of radius $\dfrac{x}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=xy+\dfrac{1}{2}\pi\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2\\&=x\left(125-\dfrac{2x+\pi x}{4}\right)+\dfrac{\pi x^2}{8}\\&=125x-\dfrac{4x^2+2\pi x^2}{8}+\dfrac{\pi x^2}{8}\\&=125x-x^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{8}\right)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the area as rectangle plus semicircle and substitutes for $y$, or equivalent merit
Finds $y=125-\dfrac{2x+\pi x}{4}$ from the perimeter, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric in the source was tick marks only; rows written by us. The source's last-but-one line had a garbled fraction; rewritten as 125x - (4x^2+2*pi*x^2)/8 + pi*x^2/8, same algebra.

solutions.latex:
For a maximum, solve $A'=0$ and test the second derivative.
$$\begin{aligned}A'&=125-2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{8}\right)x\\0&=125-\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}x\\x&=\dfrac{500}{\pi+4}\approx 70.012\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$$A''=-\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}<0$$
So $A$ is a maximum at this value of $x$.
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\max}&=125(70.012\ldots)-(70.012\ldots)^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{8}\right)\\&\approx 4375.8\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $x\approx 70.012\ldots$ and shows it is a maximum, or equivalent merit

The diagram below shows the graph of the function $f(x)=\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$.

The points $P(0,0)$ and $Q\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$ both lie on the curve.

The point $R(t,\sin t)$ is also a point on the curve between $P$ and $Q$, such that $0\le t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

\exfigure{571_q21_1}

figures.cap: graph of y=sin x with points P, R, Q and triangle PQR shaded
solution sketch: annotated diagram of triangle PQR with rectangle and trapezoid areas

parts.latex:
Show that $A$, the area of $\triangle PQR$, is given by

$$A=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin t-3\sqrt{3}\,t\right)\text{ when }t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}.$$

Find the maximum value of $A$, the area of $\triangle PQR$.

Justify your answer, leaving your answer correct to two decimal places.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{571_q21_s1}

The area of $\triangle PQR$ is the area under $PR$ plus the area under $RQ$, minus the area under $PQ$ (each a trapezium on the $x$-axis).
$$A=\dfrac{1}{2}\,t\sin t+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}-t\right)\left(\sin t+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
Expand and simplify.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}t\sin t+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin t+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}\,\pi}{3}-t\sin t-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}t\right)-\dfrac{\pi\sqrt{3}}{6}\\&=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\sin t-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}t\\&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin t-3\sqrt{3}\,t\right)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds an area that will lead to significant progress to a solution

solutions.latex:
Differentiate and find the stationary point.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin t-3\sqrt{3}\,t\right)\\\dfrac{dA}{dt}&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\cos t-3\sqrt{3}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary point where $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=0$:
$$\cos t=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{4\pi}$$
so $t=1.145\ldots$, which lies in $0\le t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dt^2}=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(-4\pi\sin t\right)$$
When $t=1.145$, $\dfrac{d^2A}{dt^2}=-0.9534<0$, so the curve is concave down and this is a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin 1.145-3\sqrt{3}\times 1.145\right)\\&\approx 0.46\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum } A\approx 0.46$$
criteria: Satisfies one criteria point. Criteria points: finds $t$; test for concavity; finds maximum $A$

meta.format_note: Checked: t = 1.1445, d2A/dt2 = -0.953, A = 0.458. A = 0 at both ends (t = 0 and t = 2pi/3), so 0.46 is the greatest value; the source does not show the end-point check.

\exfigure{638_q35_1}

The diagram above shows the circle $x^2+y^2=36$ . The point $S(x,y)$ lies on the circle in the first quadrant. $R(4,0)$ lies on the $x$-axis and $T(0,2)$ lies on the $y$-axis and $O$ is the origin. The size of $\angle SOR=\alpha$ where $0<\alpha<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ .

figures.cap: circle x^2+y^2=36 with S, R(4,0), T(0,2), angle alpha
solution sketch: right triangle with hypotenuse 6, legs x and y, angle tan^-1(2)

parts.latex: Show that the area of $\triangle SOR$ is $12\sin\alpha$ .

Hence, show that the area of the quadrilateral $ORST$ is given by:

$A=6\cos\alpha(2\tan\alpha+1)$
Find the value of $\tan\alpha$ for which the area $A$ is a maximum.
Hence, or otherwise, when the area is a maximum, find the coordinates of point $S$ in exact form.

solutions.latex:
$OS=6$ (the radius of the circle $x^2+y^2=36$) and $OR=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of }\triangle SOR&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times OS\times OR\times\sin\alpha\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 6\times 4\times\sin\alpha\\&=12\sin\alpha\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave marks only; one-row rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
$T$ is on the $y$-axis, so $\angle ROT=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\angle TOS=\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\alpha$. With $OT=2$ and $OS=6$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of }\triangle TOS&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 6\times 2\times\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\alpha\right)\\&=6\cos\alpha\end{aligned}$$
The quadrilateral $ORST$ is $\triangle SOR$ and $\triangle TOS$ together.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=12\sin\alpha+6\cos\alpha\\&=6\cos\alpha\left(2\cdot\dfrac{\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha}+1\right)\\&=6\cos\alpha(2\tan\alpha+1)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the area of $\triangle TOS$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave marks only (no rubric wording); rubric rows written by us.

solutions.latex:
Use $A=12\sin\alpha+6\cos\alpha$ and differentiate.
$$\dfrac{dA}{d\alpha}=12\cos\alpha-6\sin\alpha$$
Stationary point where $\dfrac{dA}{d\alpha}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}12\cos\alpha&=6\sin\alpha\\\tan\alpha&=2\end{aligned}$$
Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{d\alpha^2}=-12\sin\alpha-6\cos\alpha$$
When $\tan\alpha=2$, $\sin\alpha=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$ and $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$ (right-angled triangle with sides $1$, $2$, $\sqrt{5}$).
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2A}{d\alpha^2}&=-\dfrac{24}{\sqrt{5}}-\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{5}}\\&=-6\sqrt{5}\\&\approx-13.42<0\end{aligned}$$
so the area is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \tan\alpha=2\text{ gives the maximum area}$$

meta.overwritten_from_source: Source substituted into the second derivative as -6 sin - 6 cos, got +9.456 > 0 (a minimum) and still concluded maximum; d2A/dalpha2 = -12 sin(alpha) - 6 cos(alpha) = -6 sqrt(5) = -13.42 < 0 at tan(alpha) = 2, a maximum.

From part (c), $\tan\alpha=2$. For $S(x,y)$ on the circle, $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{y}{x}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{y}{x}&=2\\y&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$S$ lies on $x^2+y^2=36$:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2+4x^2&=36\\5x^2&=36\\x&=\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{5}}=\dfrac{6\sqrt{5}}{5}&&(x>0)\end{aligned}$$
and $y=2x=\dfrac{12\sqrt{5}}{5}$.
$$S\left(\dfrac{6\sqrt{5}}{5},\dfrac{12\sqrt{5}}{5}\right)$$

parts.latex: Show $A=\pi r^2+\dfrac{2V}{\pi}\left(\dfrac{2+\pi}{r}\right)$, given that $V=\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2h$.
Show that the amount of sheet metal used is minimised when $r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{V(2+\pi)}{\pi^2}}$.
Hence find the height of the tank, given that the volume of the tank is 10 cubic metres.

solutions.latex:
The volume is $V=\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2h$, so
$$h=\dfrac{2V}{\pi r^2}$$
The closed tank has two half-discs (together $\pi r^2$), half of the curved cylinder surface ($\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot2\pi rh$) and a flat rectangular top ($2r\times h$).
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \pi r^2+\pi rh+2rh \\ &= \pi r^2+\pi r\cdot\dfrac{2V}{\pi r^2}+2r\cdot\dfrac{2V}{\pi r^2} \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{2V}{r}+\dfrac{4V}{\pi r} \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{2V}{\pi}\left[\dfrac{\pi}{r}+\dfrac{2}{r}\right] \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{2V}{\pi}\left(\dfrac{2+\pi}{r}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes $A=\pi r^2+\pi rh+2rh$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. Face list added by us (the handwriting said 'half cylinder plus rectangles'); checked algebra to the printed result.

solutions.latex:
Write $A$ with negative powers of $r$ so that it can be differentiated.
$$A=\pi r^2+2Vr^{-1}+\dfrac{4V}{\pi}r^{-1}$$
$$\dfrac{dA}{dr}=2\pi r-2Vr^{-2}-\dfrac{4V}{\pi}r^{-2}$$
For stationary points, $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\pi r &= \dfrac{2V}{r^2}+\dfrac{4V}{\pi r^2} \\ 2\pi^2r^3 &= 2\pi V+4V \quad(\text{multiplying through by } \pi r^2) \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{2\pi V+4V}{2\pi^2} \\ &= \dfrac{V(\pi+2)}{\pi^2} \\ r &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{V(\pi+2)}{\pi^2}} \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative, for $r>0$:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=2\pi+4Vr^{-3}+\dfrac{8V}{\pi}r^{-3}>0$$
The graph of $A$ is concave up for all $r>0$, so this stationary point is a minimum. It is the only stationary point for $r>0$, so it is the absolute minimum, and the amount of sheet metal is minimised when $r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{V(2+\pi)}{\pi^2}}$.
criteria: Finds the value of $r$ at the stationary point, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} r &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{10(\pi+2)}{\pi^2}} \\ &\approx 1.7335\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} h &= \dfrac{2\times10}{\pi r^2} \\ &\approx 2.118\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A pipe costs \$4000/km when laid on land and \$5000/km when laid under the ocean.

In the diagram below a pipeline needs to be laid from $A$ along a coast to $B$ on an island. The pipe is to be laid in straight lines from $A$ on land along the coast until $C$ and then under the ocean to $B$.

Let $x=CD$.

\exfigure{1597_q5b_1}
Write an expression for the total price (\$$P$) of laying the cable from $A$ to $B$ via $C$ in terms of $x$.
Find the length for $x$ that will minimise the total price (\$$P$) of laying the whole pipe from $A$ to $B$ via $C$.

solutions.latex:
The land section is $AC=10-x$ km at \$4000/km, and the ocean section $CB$ is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with sides $6$ and $x$, so $CB=\sqrt{36+x^2}$ km at \$5000/km (Pythagoras' theorem).

$$P=4000(10-x)+5000\sqrt{36+x^2}$$

meta.format_note: Lengths 10 and 6 read from the source expression (figure not visible here).

solutions.latex:
$P$ is minimised where $\dfrac{dP}{dx}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dx} &= -4000+5000\times\dfrac{1}{2}(36+x^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times 2x \\ &= \dfrac{5000x}{\sqrt{36+x^2}}-4000 \end{aligned}$$

Set this to zero:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5x}{\sqrt{36+x^2}} &= 4 \\ 25x^2 &= 16(36+x^2) \\ 9x^2 &= 576 \\ x^2 &= 64 \end{aligned}$$

So $x=\pm 8$. Since $0\le x\le 10$, $x=8$ only.

First derivative test:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } x=7:\ \dfrac{dP}{dx} &\approx -204<0 &&\text{decreasing}\\ \text{At } x=9:\ \dfrac{dP}{dx} &\approx 160>0 &&\text{increasing} \end{aligned}$$

So a relative minimum occurs at $x=8$.

Check against the end points:

$$\begin{aligned} P(0) &= \$70\,000 \\ P(10) &\approx \$58\,310 \\ P(8) &= \$58\,000 \end{aligned}$$

So $x=8$ gives the absolute minimum on $[0,10]$.

Alternatively, by the second derivative test:

$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dx^2}=\dfrac{180\,000}{(36+x^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$$

which equals $180>0$ at $x=8$.

$$\therefore\ CD=8 \text{ km}$$
criteria: Solves $\dfrac{dP}{dx}=0$ to find $x=8$, or equivalent merit
Differentiates $P$ and sets the derivative to zero, or equivalent merit

2516.stem:
A rainwater tank manufacturer wants to make a new storage tank that has a standard height, to reduce the obstruction of views. The manufacturer decides that it will be a 2 metre high rectangular prism with all faces made from sheet metal, including the top and bottom, and needs to hold 6000 litres of water,

Let the other dimensions be $x$ metres and $y$ metres, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1614_q13_1}

For cost reasons, the manufacturer wants to use the least amount of area of sheet metal possible.

figures.cap: rectangular prism tank, 6000 L, height 2 m, sides x m and y m

parts.latex: Show that for the given capacity of the tank, $y=\dfrac{3}{x}$
Hence, calculate the exact dimensions of the tank that uses the least amount of area of sheet metal as possible. Show all reasoning.

solutions.latex:
Convert the capacity: $6000\text{ L}=6\text{ m}^3$.

The volume of the prism is length $\times$ width $\times$ height:
$$\begin{aligned} x\times y\times2&=6 \\ 2xy&=6 \\ y&=\dfrac{6}{2x} \\ &=\dfrac{3}{x} \end{aligned}$$

The surface area is the top and bottom plus four sides:
$$A=2(xy+2x+2y)=2xy+4x+4y$$
Substituting $y=\dfrac{3}{x}$:
$$A=4x+\dfrac{12}{x}+6$$
Differentiating:
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=4-\dfrac{12}{x^2}$$
For a minimum, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:

solutions.latex:
The volume is the cylinder plus the cube of side $2r$.
$$\pi r^2 h + (2r)^3 = 1.5$$
$$h = \dfrac{1.5 - 8r^3}{\pi r^2}$$
The coated surface is the 6 faces of the cube plus the curved surface of the cylinder. Let $S$ be this area.
$$S = 6\times(2r)^2 + 2\pi rh$$
Substituting $h$,
$$\begin{aligned} S(r) &= 24r^2 + 2\pi r\left(\dfrac{1.5 - 8r^3}{\pi r^2}\right) \\ &= 24r^2 + \dfrac{3 - 16r^3}{r} \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating,
$$S'(r) = 48r - \dfrac{3}{r^2} - 32r$$
For a stationary point, $S'(r) = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 16r &= \dfrac{3}{r^2} \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{3}{16} \end{aligned}$$
$$r = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{16}} \text{ since } r > 0$$
Test the nature using the sign of $S'(r)$.
$$\begin{aligned} S'(r) &< 0 &&\text{for } r \text{ just below } \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{16}} &&\text{decreasing}\\ S'(r) &= 0 &&\text{at } r = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{16}} &&\text{stationary}\\ S'(r) &> 0 &&\text{for } r \text{ just above } \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{16}} &&\text{increasing} \end{aligned}$$
So this is a minimum.
$$S_{\min} = 24\left(\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{16}}\right)^2 + \dfrac{3 - 16\times\frac{3}{16}}{\sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{16}}} \approx 7.86 \text{ m}^2$$
The minimum surface area is $7.86 \text{ m}^2$ (to 2 d.p.).

solutions.latex:
The volume of a cylinder is $V = \pi r^2 h$, and $V = 380$, so we make $h$ the subject.
$$380 = \pi r^2 h,\qquad h = \dfrac{380}{\pi r^2}$$
Substitute into $A = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi rh$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r\left(\dfrac{380}{\pi r^2}\right) \\ &= 2\pi r^2 + \dfrac{760\pi r}{\pi r^2} \\ &= 2\pi r^2 + \dfrac{760}{r} \end{aligned}$$

Differentiate $A$ twice.
$$\dfrac{dA}{dr} = 4\pi r - \dfrac{760}{r^2},\qquad \dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2} = 4\pi + \dfrac{1520}{r^3}$$
Since $r > 0$, $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2} > 0$, therefore $A$ has a minimum value.

The minimum occurs when $\dfrac{dA}{dr} = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4\pi r - \dfrac{760}{r^2} &= 0 \\ 4\pi r^3 &= 760 \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{760}{4\pi} \\ r &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{760}{4\pi}} \\ &\approx 3.925 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ r \approx 3.925 \text{ m}$$
